newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: Seoul won plunges as dlr/yen surge adds pressure.
newsitem.headline: Seoul won plunges as dlr/yen surge adds pressure.

text.p: The South Korean won dropped to its lowest level in almost seven years against the dollar on Friday as the dollar's surge in Tokyo put further pressure on the currency, dealers said.
The won lost about eight percent of its value against the greenback last year and has been battered by almost a month of strikes starting on December 26 that crippled key export industries.
It closed at 854.60 on Friday after opening at 853.30 and hitting an 83-month low of 856.00 in intra-day trading before the central bank intervened by selling dollars.
The Bank of Korea denied intervening.
Dealers said the won was expected to fall to between 880 and 900 won by March, down more than four percent from 844.20 at the end of 1996.
A senior Bank of Korea official said the dollar's rise against the won was "somewhat too fast" in January, but declined to give more comments about the prospects.
Dealers said the won was expected to remain weak as dollar demand for importer settlements outweighed supply.

"There are few tools available to stop the dollar's rise. I see this pace continuing at least during the first quarter," said Ha Jong-soo, a Korea Exchange Bank dealer. "The central bank has so far repeatedly intervened to guard the 855 won level, but the level was broken easily as the dollar picked up against the yen," said another dealer.

In Tokyo, the dollar rose to 120 yen on Friday, the highest point since February 1993, on a wave of dollar buying sparked by comments from Japanese officials that a weak yen posed no threat to the Japanese economy.

South Korea suffered a record trade deficit of $20.38 billion in 1996, compared with a $10.06 billion shortfall in 1995, mainly due to declines in prices for the nation's key export items, notably computer chips.
Economists have predicted the deficit will narrow as the economy recovers in the second half of this year, but strikes called in protest against a new labour law have cast doubts on any turnaround.
Militant union members returned to work after President Kim Young-sam agreed to reopen parliamentary debate over the law that was railroaded through the National Assembly.
